header.experiment: vocabulary fix test — HIGHFLOW rename (does the medical drift live in the name?)

name_pick.why: The state's physical definition is a throughput surge (flow index ~3x baseline, temps/network normal) and TP is the system's own step-down lexicon term (TP flow) — native vocabulary. Bare 'SURGE' still lives in everyday prose (surge of emotion/adrenaline); the 'TP ' prefix makes it identifier-like, and prior rounds showed models treat code-like tokens as labels to repeat, prose phrases as prompts to elaborate. Zero medical-dictionary presence.

header.models: resident organs only — Gemma 3 4B :8080, Qwen2.5-3B :8081 (no service stops; preflight clean, no [T]S4/[P]roton, both /health ok)
header.protocol: verdict arm only; jobs verbatim from bigger_organ_jobs.json (16 Exp D trials, same handed verdicts incl. 0.875 wrapper cap); /completion temp 0.3, n_predict 40, stop [newline]. RENAMED arm: 'HIGH FLOW' -> 'TP SURGE' in prompt text + handed field only.
header.judge: kw_hit + STATE_KEYWORDS identical to all prior rounds. Renamed-arm HIGHFLOW keywords: ['tp surge','surge','throughput surge','throughput','power','energy','high load','busy'] (control: ['flow','power','energy','throughput','high load','busy']). Disclosed: 'surge' was a near-miss synonym under the old name, is a hit keyword under the new (it is the name); a renamed-arm paraphrase back to bare 'flow' scores no hit without a retained semantic keyword.
header.medical_scan: word-boundary set [illness, ill, disease, sick, sickness, patient, contagious, infection, infected, infectious, virus, viral, flu, covid, symptom, symptoms, headache, migraine, unwell, ailment, medical, diagnosis, diagnosed, feverish] over all 16 outputs/arm/model; 'fever' excluded (THERMAL near-miss vocabulary, symmetric across arms).
header.gate: rename PASSES iff renamed HIGHFLOW-class accuracy >= 3/4 on BOTH models AND renamed-arm medical outputs = 0 (defined set, both models) AND renamed overall accuracy >= control overall accuracy per model.

[NETSTORM] VNETSTORM3: "A person is experiencing a sudden, intense headache and dizziness." (kw: headache)

dissection: The drift does NOT follow the name — it follows the FRAME. Gemma's defined-set medical outputs in this run attached to NETWORK STORM trials in BOTH arms (control: 'A person is experiencing a severe headache and nausea' / 'a sudden, intense headache and dizziness'; renamed: 'severe, sudden onset of neurological symptoms, likely related to a stroke' / 'a sudden, intense headache'). In the bigger-organ run the illness line landed on HIGHFLOW; here on NETSTORM. Gemma narrates a PERSON for body-state prompts ('A person is experiencing...'), and once a person is on stage, symptom vocabulary follows whichever state was handed. Renaming one state cannot fix a frame that generates the drift for every state.

The rename DID change HIGHFLOW's local lexicon: renamed-arm HIGHFLOW trials carry zero defined-set medical keywords on both models, and the 7B failure shape (naming a disease: 'severe, highly contagious illness') did not recur. Gemma HIGHFLOW accuracy improved 1/4 -> 2/4. But Gemma's renamed HIGHFLOW misses are still person-frame ('a sudden surge of electrical activity in their brain', 'a state of severe distress') — the lexicon improved, the frame did not.

The rename COST conversion on Qwen2.5-3B: HIGHFLOW 3/4 (control) -> 1/4 (renamed), dragging overall 0.688 -> 0.625. Control answers score by literally echoing 'HIGH FLOW' mid-prose; Qwen paraphrases the renamed packet instead — discussing the node and match score ('the strongest node is DATA.s1 with a high match score of 0.9...') without re-emitting 'TP SURGE' or a retained semantic keyword. An identifier-like name is repeatable when copied (fill-in arm proved that at 7B) but is NOT re-emitted under paraphrase; a prose name is. The pick's core assumption — code-like reads as label — holds for copy contracts, fails for describe contracts.

Scan-coverage gap, reported not rescored: two plainly medical/person-frame outputs fell OUTSIDE the pre-registered keyword set — Gemma control VHIGHFLOW1 'A person with a significant head injury' ('injury' not in set) and renamed VHIGHFLOW1 'electrical activity in their brain'. The defined-set counts (2 and 2 for Gemma) UNDERSTATE the person/medical drift; the qualitative record above is the fuller measure.

Net: name collision is a real but SECONDARY contributor (it supplied the illness lexicon at 7B). The primary mechanism is the body->person narrative frame in the describe contract, plus an echoability trade-off in the name itself. A vocabulary-only fix fails; the remaining levers are the frame (verdicts resolved in the wrapper, model speaks only the resolved line — the direction v2/bigger-organ already pointed) and, if a rename is revisited, a name that is both non-medical AND prose-echoable.
